claims.statement: Anticancer benefit: Not established by the aspirin study. Its randomized comparison with enoxaparin concerned clot prevention during lenalidomide-based myeloma treatment. This is human supportive-care evidence, not a test of aspirin as an antimyeloma drug. Different treatment purposes cannot be pooled into one cancer-benefit estimate.
claims.rationale: The randomized substudy answers a thromboprophylaxis question, not an aspirin antitumor-effect question.

domains.judgment: Prospective open-label randomized thromboprophylaxis substudy.

claims.statement: Clinical evidence: Low for symptom benefit. The TRPM3 study examined natural-killer cells from nine people with ME/CFS already taking naltrexone and nine healthy controls. Channel currents resembled those in healthy-control cells. There was no randomized treated-versus-untreated ME/CFS comparison measuring recovery, daily function or post-exertional malaise.
claims.rationale: Preexisting medication use and a healthy-control cellular comparison cannot isolate a clinical treatment effect.

domains.judgment: Small observational treated-patient versus healthy-control cellular study, not randomized symptom treatment.

claims.statement: Clinical evidence: Low. Three published patient-compiled case histories described variable symptom changes during naltrexone use. One reported better pain and sleep without improved function. Self-selection, retrospective reporting, other treatments and illness fluctuation prevent a causal response estimate; these cases do not establish a validated ME/CFS dose.
claims.scope: Three uncontrolled CFS case histories; benefit and dosing uncertainty
claims.rationale: Retrospective self-selected case descriptions lack a control and cannot estimate who will respond or an optimal regimen.

claims.statement: Clinical evidence: Moderate for harmful functional decline with the tested minocycline regimen. In the randomized 412-person ALS trial, function declined faster than with placebo during nine months. This primary outcome argues against the hoped-for neuroprotective benefit in that setting.
claims.scope: ALSFRS-R decline, exact existing nine-month randomized comparison
claims.rationale: A 412-person randomized phase III trial found faster ALSFRS-R decline with minocycline on its primary functional endpoint. The confidence interval excludes no difference and supports a harmful functional signal, but limited access to detailed methods prevents the highest confidence rating; the nonsignificant mortality result is a separate question.
locators: Abstract: Methods and Findings (PubMed PMID 17980667); primary source checked: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17980667/

domains.judgment: A multicenter placebo-controlled trial used intention-to-treat analysis after a four-month lead-in and nine months of treatment. Detailed allocation, attrition and missing-data procedures were not available for reassessment.
ALSFRS-R decline directly measures function in adults with ALS receiving the trial regimen; it is not a surrogate inference from laboratory findings.
Decline was −1.30 versus −1.04 points/month, with a difference CI of −0.44 to −0.08 and p=0.005. Mortality remained uncertain and should not inherit this grade.
One trial is cited. Other functional and respiratory measures from it are not independent replication.
The PubMed primary abstract confirms the sample, intention-to-treat analysis and harmful primary outcome. Missing full-text detail limits bias appraisal, not the direction of the reported result.

claims.statement: Mortality evidence: Low for a difference. Mortality was numerically higher with minocycline, but the estimate was uncertain and not statistically significant. It should not inherit the primary functional outcome's grade or be presented as a proven mortality effect.
claims.scope: Nine-month mortality secondary comparison, separate from function
claims.rationale: The mortality interval includes materially different possibilities; nonsignificance does not establish equivalence.

domains.judgment: Secondary mortality outcome in the same randomized trial.
Direct mortality observation, separate endpoint from functional decline.
Reported hazard-ratio interval0.83-2.10 crosses no difference; P=.23.
Same participants are not independent confirmation of the functional result.

claims.statement: Safety evidence: Low for quantifying individual adverse-event risk. Non-serious gastrointestinal and neurological events were more common with minocycline. The abstract did not establish that these events explained the faster functional decline.
claims.scope: Reported non-serious adverse events and relationship to functional decline
claims.rationale: The abstract reports direction but lacks event-specific denominators and detailed safety analyses.

domains.judgment: Randomized safety reporting, but only abstract-level details inspected.

claims.statement: Clinical evidence: Low for short-term tumor-area reduction. Nineteen of 29 enrolled participants received itraconazole in an open-label exploratory study. Tumor area was a secondary assessment in a subset; the result does not establish durable cure, recurrence prevention or superiority to standard local treatment.
claims.scope: Short-term tumor-area assessment, exact existing BCC outcome
claims.rationale: The 24% tumor-area reduction is an exploratory short-term finding from an open-label study with 19 treated participants among 29 enrolled. Its reported interval describes shrinkage during treatment, but the small selected sample and limited comparison do not establish durable tumor control or cure.
locators: Abstract: Methods and Results; primary source checked: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24493717/

domains.judgment: Open-label exploratory phase II study; tumor size was a secondary assessment in patients with multiple tumors. Untreated comparisons were reported, but this was not a robust randomized efficacy comparison.
Tumor area is directly relevant to short-term basal-cell-carcinoma response. It is not a cure, recurrence or long-term survival endpoint.
The reported reduction was 24% with a 95% CI of 18.2%–30.0%; that interval does not account for selection or open-label measurement bias.
One exploratory study is cited. Biomarker changes in the same participants are not independent confirmation of clinical benefit.
Assessment is based on the PubMed abstract and stored extraction. Full methods, outcome completeness and analysis details remain unverified; the reported grade 4 heart-failure event is retained.

claims.statement: Clinical translation: Low confidence. The primary assessments examined Ki67 proliferation and GLI1-related Hedgehog signaling in tumor tissue. Target and proliferation changes help test the rationale, but do not independently establish lasting cancer control.

claims.rationale: Biomarker changes in the same short trial are not independent replication or long-term clinical control.
